name: Oral cysteine / NAC for pigment
lead: Oral N-acetylcysteine (NAC) and L-cysteine are supplements that some people take as a route to lighter, more even-toned skin. The idea is a chain: cysteine is the raw material the body uses to make glutathione, and glutathione is the compound most often taken by mouth in skin-whitening circles, so supplying the precursor is thought to support a brighter complexion.[1][2][3]

NAC is a cysteine prodrug that is established in medicine as an antidote for paracetamol (acetaminophen) overdose and as a mucolytic, and it is sold over the counter as a supplement. It is valued by users as a cheaper, better-absorbed alternative to swallowing glutathione itself, which Wikipedia notes is poorly available by mouth because digestive proteases break it down.[1][2]

Skin-lightening agents in general are described as acting on melanin in several ways, such as inhibiting tyrosinase or limiting melanosome transfer, and a 2019 summary notes it was unclear whether glutathione itself lightens skin.[3] No published human study of oral NAC or cysteine for skin pigmentation was located.
infobox: Glutathione, the most common oral skin-whitening supplement[3]

paras: In appearance and skin-lightening discussions, oral NAC or cysteine is used as an inexpensive glutathione booster, with the stated goal of a lighter or more even skin tone.[2][3] Proponents reason that cysteine availability limits glutathione production and that glutathione status influences how much melanin is made; this is the reasoning behind the practice rather than a result reported in the cited reference articles.[1][2]

The established uses are treating paracetamol overdose, where it helps restore glutathione to neutralize a toxic metabolite, and thinning mucus in chronic lung conditions. A 2013 Cochrane review found no evidence of benefit in cystic fibrosis. It is on the WHO List of Essential Medicines.[1]

Because NAC supplies cysteine, it can replenish intracellular glutathione stores.[1][2] Wikipedia adds that its effects are not fully explained by glutathione alone, since it may also act through hydrogen sulfide production.[1] Wikipedia's glutathione article cites work describing NAC as a cysteine prodrug that helps replenish cellular glutathione, and notes that glutathione taken directly is poorly available because it is broken down in the gut and cells lack a dedicated transporter.[2]

Wikipedia's overview of skin whitening lists the ways lighteners can reduce melanin: blocking tyrosinase, reducing its production or activation, scavenging melanin precursors, preventing melanosome transfer, breaking down existing melanin, or destroying melanocytes.[3]
No studies found of oral cysteine or NAC for skin pigmentation or lightening. For the related supplement glutathione, a 2019 summary reports it remained unclear whether it lightens skin.[3]

Oral NAC is less well tolerated than intravenous use because of taste and odor, with nausea, vomiting, rash and fever reported. Intravenous use has caused rash, hives and itching, and about 3 to 6 percent of people have had a severe anaphylaxis-like reaction. Oral bioavailability is about 6 to 10 percent.[1] Separately, the Philippine government advises against intravenous glutathione for whitening because of possible side effects.[3]

lore.intro: Oral NAC and cysteine appear in skin-lightening discussions as lower-cost routes to glutathione, usually alongside glutathione pills, vitamin C and topical brighteners.[2][3]

claims.claim: Taking NAC or cysteine raises glutathione and lightens skin
claims.believers: Proponents reason that cysteine is the limiting precursor for glutathione, that oral glutathione is poorly absorbed, and that NAC is a more bioavailable way to raise it, with glutathione linked to lighter pigment.
claims.experts: Acetylcysteine is documented to replenish glutathione in overdose treatment, and glutathione is the most common oral whitening agent, but no published studies were located testing NAC or cysteine for pigment, and it is unclear whether glutathione lightens skin.[1][2][3]

card.summary: A glutathione-precursor supplement claimed to lighten skin, with established medical uses but no located pigment studies.
card.note: Oral use commonly causes nausea or vomiting; pigment effect is untested in sources reviewed.

quick.overview:
N-acetylcysteine is a medicine and supplement that supplies cysteine, a building block of glutathione. Some people take it in the hope of lightening pigment.

The sources reviewed contain no study of NAC or cysteine for skin pigment, and Wikipedia's article on the drug does not mention it.
quick.mechanism: It raises cysteine availability and so can replenish glutathione; the link from glutathione to visible skin tone is the claim, not an established finding.
quick.risks: Oral use can cause nausea, vomiting, rash and fever. Oral bioavailability is only about 6 to 10 percent.

chain: Oral NAC or cysteine supplies cysteine

angle.text: People take oral NAC or cysteine hoping to raise glutathione availability and thereby brighten skin tone or fade uneven pigment. It is typically discussed alongside glutathione itself, vitamin C and topical brighteners as part of a complexion routine.
